conclusion: Point-to-point interface-owned routes avoid the raw AF_ROUTE GET/DELETE ownership race. Prefer two sequential fresh owned utuns, DNS then HTTP, after verifying complete first-interface cleanup. In-place retarget is possible only with explicit route readback and failure handling; ioctl success alone cannot qualify it. Neither route creation nor close is a transactional success guarantee.

facts.fact: SIOCSIFDSTADDR updates the peer field, then holds rnh_lock across old-peer rtinit_locked DELETE and new-peer ADD when IFA_ROUTE is set. rtinit_locked checks rt_ifa pointer identity and refuses deletion of static routes under the same rnh_lock. Another route writer cannot replace a route between that identity check and deletion.

Retarget ignores both rtinit_locked return values, preserves IFA_ROUTE, and does no route operation at all if IFA_ROUTE was clear. SIOCGIFDSTADDR may report the new peer even if the new route is missing; the metadata update is earlier than the locked route operations and the operation is not rollback-atomic.

SIOCAIFADDR can configure local, peer and mask together. in_ifinit creates the point-to-point RTF_HOST route, sets IFA_ROUTE only on successful ADD, but converts EEXIST to success. A fresh interface still needs actual route readback.

Generic ADD on an existing cloned destination can delete that clone and retry. Existing noncloned routes normally cause EEXIST. This is not blanket protection of every foreign route: candidate admission needs a fresh/exclusive guest routing context and absence of a conflicting exact destination, including clones, before configuration.

Closing the owned utun control socket invokes family cleanup: remove its IPv4 addresses with SIOCDIFADDR then detach protocol and interface. Address deletion scrubs the route through the same rtinit_locked identity/static checks. Cleanup failures are logged; disconnect returns0; final interface detach is asynchronous. close success is not evidence that interface/route cleanup completed.
SIOCGIFADDR, SIOCGIFDSTADDR and SIOCGIFNETMASK read back address metadata only. None proves the corresponding destination route exists.

proposed_bounded_contract: Use only a newly allocated owned utun, exactly one IPv4 address local10.0.2.15/32 and exactly one unicast peer. No explicit RTM_ADD/DELETE, default route, host-controller route, firewall or resolver configuration mutation.

Before either interface configuration, establish the exclusive guest network-management context and inspect routing state for conflicting local/peer addresses and exact destination routes, including cloned entries. A preflight query alone is not a race-proof ownership lease; no other guest route/configuration actor may operate during the finite test.

Configure DNS phase peer10.0.2.3; read back interface name/index, POINTTOPOINT/UP state, local/peer/mask and actual active exact host route on that index using a separately qualified read-only observer. Use PF_ROUTE protocol0 if choosing routing-socket GET; the held mutating prototype remains excluded.

Use real Darwin UDP socket DNS with bounded input, query/response correlation and validated A selection. Close/reap every DNS socket/worker before interface teardown or retarget. Readback or offline packet bytes are not DNS runtime proof.

Preferred: close the DNS utun, verify disappearance of its name/index and associated address/route, then create a fresh owned HTTP utun with the selected public A as peer and the same local /32. Revalidate actual route/metadata; start a new Darwin TCP socket only afterward. Carry correct hostname in the HTTP request; changing A requires a new explicitly bounded phase.

If reusing an interface instead, verify old-route absence and new exact route/interface after SIOCSIFDSTADDR, including failures; old/new operations are serialized but their errors are suppressed. Do not repair failure with raw AF_ROUTE deletion.

Close application sockets before owned control fd. Bound and record actual interface and route disappearance, compare unrelated guest routing/default state to baseline, preserve any cleanup uncertainty as failure and use existing root-owned verified-Linux recovery. No public boot or success claim follows from this source note.
